knowledge_graph.title: Blount's disease
knowledge_graph.description: Blount's disease is a growth disorder of the tibia which causes the lower leg to angle inward, resembling a bowleg. It is also known as "tibia vara".

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, Blount's disease can be treated and often cured, particularly when caught early. Treatment options vary depending on the severity and age of the individual, but can include bracing, guided growth procedures, or osteotomy (bone correction surgery).
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, Blount's disease can be treated and often cured, particularly when caught early

list.title: Early intervention is key:
list.snippet: In younger children with infantile Blount's disease, bracing can be effective in straightening the legs as they grow.

list.title: Surgery may be necessary:
list.snippet: If bracing is not successful or if the condition is diagnosed later or is more severe, surgery may be required.

list.title: Osteotomy:
list.snippet: A surgical procedure where the bone is cut and realigned, often with internal or external fixation to hold the bone in place while it heals.

list.title: Guided growth:
list.snippet: A procedure where plates or staples are used to guide the bone's growth and correct the deformity over time.

list.title: Good prognosis:
list.snippet: With appropriate treatment, Blount's disease can be corrected, and the leg should function normally and appear straight.

text_blocks.snippet: Blount's disease, also known as tibial vara, is a condition where the lower leg bows outward, primarily due to an abnormality in the growth plate of the tibia (shinbone). While the exact cause is unknown, it's believed to be a combination of genetic, environmental, and mechanical factors.
snippet_highlighted_words: the exact cause is unknown, it's believed to be a combination of genetic, environmental, and mechanical factors

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of the contributing factors:

list.snippet: Blount's disease tends to run in families, suggesting a genetic component.
It's more common in certain ethnicities, particularly African American children, according to Columbia Orthopedic Surgery.
Individuals with a family history of the condition are at a higher risk.

Early Walking: Infants who begin walking very early (before 12 months) may be at increased risk because their bones are not yet fully developed to withstand the pressure of weight-bearing, according to the Nicklaus Children's Hospital.
Obesity: Extra weight on the tibia can contribute to abnormal bone growth, making overweight or obese children more susceptible, says Columbia Orthopedic Surgery.
Rapid Weight Gain: Adolescents experiencing rapid weight gain may also be at a higher risk.
Low Vitamin D levels: may play a role in some cases.
Metabolic disorders, such as rickets, can also contribute to the condition.
Infections: or trauma to the proximal tibia can also be a cause.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, Blount's disease is a complex condition influenced by a combination of factors. While the exact cause is unknown, genetic predisposition, early or excessive weight-bearing, and potential metabolic or injury-related issues are believed to play a role, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

related_questions.question: What is the difference between rickets and Blount's disease?
related_questions.snippet: Unlike rickets, cupping, fraying and splaying of metaphyses are absent in Blount's disease. Rickets is associated with diffuse bowing throughout the bone rather than the characteristic proximal tibial deformity with medial beaking of Blount's disease.

related_questions.question: At what age should bow legs be corrected?

text_blocks.snippet: Most cases of bow legs in children, known as genu varum, are normal and resolve on their own by the age of 3 or 4. If the bowing persists beyond this age, or if it's severe, asymmetrical, or associated with pain or other symptoms, it may indicate a condition requiring further evaluation and potentially treatment.

list.title: Common in infancy and early childhood:
list.snippet: Bowing is a normal developmental stage as babies' legs adapt to the womb position and their weight-bearing development.

list.title: Typically self-corrects:
list.snippet: Most children's legs will naturally straighten between 18 months and 3-4 years of age as they grow and develop.

list.title: No intervention needed:
list.snippet: If the bowing is mild to moderate, symmetrical, and not causing pain or mobility issues, it's usually part of normal development, and no treatment is required.

list.title: Beyond age 3:
list.snippet: If the bowing persists beyond the age of 3, it's important to have it evaluated by a healthcare professional.

list.title: Severe or worsening bowing:
list.snippet: If the bowing is severe or appears to be getting worse, especially after the age of 3, it should be assessed.

list.title: Asymmetrical bowing:
list.snippet: If the bowing is significantly more pronounced in one leg than the other, it could indicate a problem.

list.title: Associated symptoms:
list.snippet: If the child experiences pain, limited range of motion, or difficulty walking or running, a doctor should be consulted.

list.title: Underlying conditions:
list.snippet: If there's a family history of bow legs or if the child has a condition like Blount's disease or rickets, it's crucial to seek early evaluation.

list.title: Observation:
list.snippet: In many cases, if the bowing is mild and not causing issues, observation may be all that's needed, allowing the legs to straighten naturally.

list.title: Bracing:
list.snippet: In some cases, bracing may be recommended to help guide the legs into a more normal alignment as they grow.

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: If the bowing is caused by a condition like rickets, medication may be prescribed to address the underlying issue.

list.title: Surgery:
list.snippet: In more severe or complex cases, surgical intervention, such as osteotomy or guided growth surgery, may be considered.

text_blocks.snippet: Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial for optimal outcomes. If you have any concerns about your child's leg alignment, consult with a healthcare professional, preferably an orthopedic specialist, for proper evaluation and guidance.

text_blocks.snippet: Blount's disease, also known as tibia vara, is a growth disorder that affects the shinbone (tibia) in children, causing the lower leg to curve inward, creating a bow-legged appearance. It occurs when the growth plate near the knee experiences excessive pressure, disrupting normal bone development and leading to uneven growth. This condition can be seen in infants and adolescents, and if left untreated, it can lead to pain, arthritis, and difficulty walking.
snippet_highlighted_words: a growth disorder that affects the shinbone (tibia) in children, causing the lower leg to curve inward, creating a bow-legged appearance

list.title: Abnormal Growth Plate:
list.snippet: The growth plate at the top of the tibia is responsible for leg lengthening. In Blount's disease, this growth plate experiences excessive pressure, especially on the inner (medial) side, causing uneven growth.

list.title: Bowing of the Leg:
list.snippet: The uneven growth results in the lower leg curving outward, creating a bow-legged appearance.

list.title: Age of Onset:
list.snippet: Blount's disease can be classified into two main types: infantile (early-onset), occurring in children under 3, and adolescent, occurring after age 10.

list.title: Early vs. Late Onset:
list.snippet: Infantile Blount's disease is often associated with early walking and can affect both legs. Adolescent Blount's disease is more common in overweight or obese individuals and can be unilateral (affecting one leg).

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Besides the visible bowing, symptoms may include knee pain, instability, in-toeing (feet angling inward), and difficulty walking.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Diagnosis involves a physical exam, observation of gait, and X-rays to assess the leg's alignment and the growth plate's condition.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment options vary depending on the severity and age of the child, ranging from bracing to surgery to correct the deformity.

list.title: Complications:
list.snippet: Untreated Blount's disease can lead to arthritis, leg length discrepancies, and further disability.
